phys.org/news/2026-11-hidden-leaf-dynami.excerpt: From space, the Amazon rainforest looks like an unbroken expanse of green. But a new study conducted by researchers from the School of Biological Sciences at The University of Hong Kong (HKU), together with international collaborators, reveals seasonal leaf changes hidden within this seemingly constant canopy. Largely undetected by conventional satellite observations, these changes have significant implications for estimating the rainforest's carbon uptake.

phys.org/news/2026-11-upwelling-panama-f.excerpt: A year after scientists at the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute (STRI) in Panama reported the first recorded failure of the Gulf of Panama's seasonal upwelling, a follow-up study now documents how that failure moved through the system, from wind to plankton to fish to exports, using records that fishing companies rarely share.

phys.org/news/2026-11-baltic-sea-reveal-.excerpt: Like humans, the ocean breathes. And when it does, a new study shows that far more is happening than researchers have previously assumed. "We can see that the ocean's chemical breathing is far more diverse and dynamic than we previously thought," says Mehrshad Foroughan, a postdoctoral researcher at the Department of Biology who is the first author of the new study.

phys.org/news/2026-11-shells-insights-el.title: How shells are made: New insights elucidate crystals' uptake of 'disruptors'
phys.org/news/2026-11-shells-insights-el.excerpt: For a mollusk to build its shell, it uses brittle chalk—crystalline calcite—which must take in other materials to make the chalk stronger. That process of incorporation has long been a mystery—one that Professor Lara Estroff has been working on for her entire career.

phys.org/news/2026-11-microscopic-chambe.title: Microscopic chambers reveal how bacteria navigate tight spots
phys.org/news/2026-11-microscopic-chambe.excerpt: New York University researchers have built a way to observe bacteria as they typically live: in confinement. The research, published in the journal Small, introduces microscopic traps that mimic the tiny crevices where bacteria actually live—for instance, in soil or in our mouths.

phys.org/news/2026-11-reveals-dual-roles.title: Study reveals dual roles for ATRX in nucleosome remodeling and histone chaperoning
phys.org/news/2026-11-reveals-dual-roles.excerpt: ATRX is an ATP-dependent chromatin remodeler that helps maintain genome stability. Mutations in ATRX cause ATR-X syndrome and are found in several types of cancer. ATRX is best known for working with the histone chaperone DAXX to deposit the histone variant H3.3 in heterochromatin, where it helps maintain gene silencing and chromatin integrity. However, how ATRX regulates its own ATPase activity, uses ATP to remodel nucleosomes and functions in accessible chromatin remains unclear.

phys.org/news/2026-11-magnets-extreme-vo.title: No magnets needed: Extreme voltage drives completely new kind of Hall effect
phys.org/news/2026-11-magnets-extreme-vo.excerpt: The Hall effect, a physical phenomenon in which a current arises perpendicular to a voltage applied across a material, has been of particular interest to physicists since it was discovered more than a century ago. Over time, physicists have broadened their understanding of the Hall effect, describing quantum and anomalous versions that appear under nonclassical conditions. Recently, Rice University's Qimiao Si published a paper in Physical Review Letters describing a new variant called the fully nonequilibrium response that once again expands how physicists understand the Hall effect.

phys.org/news/2026-11-oxidative-stress-c.title: Oxidative stress alters and 'clogs' grass pollen allergens, study finds
phys.org/news/2026-11-oxidative-stress-c.excerpt: Medical experts suspect that high levels of air pollution exacerbate the symptoms of hay fever patients. Researchers at the Max Planck Institute for Chemistry in Mainz (MPIC) have now solved a chemical puzzle: When pollen allergens encounter peroxynitrite, the allergens undergo surprisingly systematic changes. New chemical groups are attached at specific exposed sites on the protein. In addition, it "glues" or links the allergens together. The findings are published in the journal Free Radical Research.

phys.org/news/2026-11-tool-climate-resha.title: New modeling tool sheds light on how climate change could reshape marine ecosystems
phys.org/news/2026-11-tool-climate-resha.excerpt: A new high-resolution modeling tool is offering one of the clearest pictures yet of how climate change could affect a vital part of the marine food chain in Northwest European seas. The machine learning model developed by researchers at the University of Strathclyde predicts how zooplankton—tiny drifting animals that underpin marine ecosystems—could respond to changing ocean conditions over the coming decades.

phys.org/news/2026-11-fiber-laser-combin.title: New fiber laser combines ultrashort pulses with broad spectrum and stable output
phys.org/news/2026-11-fiber-laser-combin.excerpt: Femtosecond lasers produce pulses lasting only quadrillionths of a second. Their speed makes them useful for imaging rapid processes, sampling high-frequency signals and measuring distance or time with high precision. For these applications, a laser must provide not only short pulses and a broad spectrum but also stable output. Fluctuations in pulse intensity or timing can reduce image quality and measurement accuracy.

phys.org/news/2026-11-bacteria-membranes.title: Bacteria split their membranes to kill infected cells and block viral spread, study shows
phys.org/news/2026-11-bacteria-membranes.excerpt: A new study reveals a previously unknown bacterial immune mechanism in which the signaling molecule 2′,3′-cGAMP triggers the splitting of the bacterial membrane into two distinct bilayers, leading to the death of infected cells and preventing further phage propagation.

phys.org/news/2026-11-significance-stats.title: Significance and stats: Massive sample sizes do not guarantee reliable findings, study suggests
phys.org/news/2026-11-significance-stats.excerpt: The increasing use of large health care databases has exposed a fundamental statistical weakness: the assumption that bigger data sets automatically produce more reliable findings. A review of a large health care database associated with vaccination and cancer in the International Journal of Medical Engineering and Informatics shows that in practice, standard statistical methods can generate misleading levels of significance, masking underlying flaws in the data.

phys.org/news/2026-11-countries-ways-saf.excerpt: Countries have agreed on new measures to speed up efforts aimed at preventing the harmful effects of chemical products on health and the environment, the U.N. said.

phys.org/news/2026-11-proteins-ancient-v.excerpt: Much of our genome contains mobile pieces or "transposable elements": pieces of DNA that spread and accumulated over millions of years, some originating from ancient viruses. Although many are no longer mobile, their sequences can influence when nearby genes switch on or off.

phys.org/news/2026-11-reshapes-remotely-.title: Engineering study reshapes understanding of remotely triggered earthquakes
phys.org/news/2026-11-reshapes-remotely-.excerpt: Understanding earthquake mechanisms and mitigating earthquake hazards remain a critical global challenge. For decades, seismologists have observed that seismic waves of large earthquakes can trigger seismic activity at distances of thousands of kilometers—a phenomenon known as remote (dynamic) triggering. Yet two puzzles persisted: Why do some triggered events occur long after the seismic waves have passed? And why do Rayleigh waves, which carry lower shear stresses than Love waves, appear more effective at triggering?

universetoday.com/articles/new-research-.excerpt: Scientists using the W.M. Keck Observatory's HIRISE spectrometer have revealed new information about the origin of Europa's sodium cloud.

universetoday.com/articles/detecting-pri.title: Detecting Primordial Black Holes By The Stars They Destroy
universetoday.com/articles/detecting-pri.excerpt: Astrophysicists wonder if primordial black holes could be part, or maybe all, of dark matter. They're theorized to have formed immediately after the Big Bang from pockets of dense matter. New research shows how they might be detected: in the bbright flash generated by the stars they consume from the inside out.

universetoday.com/articles/ultra-thin-ra.title: Ultra-Thin "Rainbow" Sails Could Power Spacecraft and Shade the Earth
universetoday.com/articles/ultra-thin-ra.excerpt: For years, whimsically minded space enthusiasts have been dreaming of sailing across the vastness of the void on beams of sunlight. Photons, the massless particles that make up those beams of sunlight, still carry momentum, and can therefore impart a gentle push when they bounce off a surface. This force is the concept behind “solar sailing”, which has been having a bit of a moment in the last decade as several proof-of-concept flights have shown it is indeed actually feasible. Now a new paper, available in pre-print on arXiv from researchers at the Rochester Institute of Technology (RIT), has unveiled a clever technique that will allow these giant sails to steer sideways using a technology more commonly associated with flat-screen displays.

universetoday.com/articles/lisas-gravita.title: LISA's Gravitational Wave Detections Could Reveal Exoplanets
universetoday.com/articles/lisas-gravita.excerpt: LISA, the ESA's Laser Interferometry Space Antenna, is being built to detect gravitational waves emitted when massive objects spiral together and merge. New research shows that exoplanets can exert a small but perceptible tug on those objects, leaving a signature on the gravitational waves. In some cases, LISA should be able to detect their signatures.

universetoday.com/articles/bacteria-and-.title: Bacteria and Nuclear Power Could Grow Ready-Made Homes on Mars Before Astronauts Arrive
universetoday.com/articles/bacteria-and-.excerpt: As we gear up to eventually land a human on Mars, more and more ideas are coming out about how to prepare for that. A recent one from Pioneer Labs, a research institute founded by bioengineer Erika DeBenedictis to develop biological technologies for space exploration, is now available on arXiv, without any plans to release it in a paid journal as part of the “Open Science” policy of The Astera Institute, who funded the research. It details “Mars Seed” - a new architecture that is self-contained and can produce a full 870 sq meters of pressurized habitat using nothing but Martian inputs within roughly every four Earth years.

First identified in the Euclid Wide Survey (EWS), the object was confirmed to be a quasar by subsequent observations with some of the most powerful telescopes on the ground and in space.

phys.org/news/2026-11-workplace-absentee.excerpt: Temporary disability is a cornerstone of the public Social Security system. It is a right for all workers who fall ill and a social security benefit designed primarily to protect those who are sick, enabling them to receive medical treatment and recover or improve their condition while ensuring they have sufficient income during periods in which they are unable to work.

phys.org/news/2026-11-conversion-tool-qu.title: New light-conversion tool could help speed up quantum computing

phys.org/news/2026-11-ai-host-big-math-p.excerpt: For many, the year 2026 will be remembered as the one when mathematics had an identity crisis and forever changed. Frontier (cutting-edge) AI models made by OpenAI and Anthropic made stunning progress on hundreds of open problems that have baffled mathematicians for decades—and centuries in some cases.

phys.org/news/2026-11-violin-physical-ch.title: Do a violin's physical characteristics really improve with regular playing?
phys.org/news/2026-11-violin-physical-ch.excerpt: There is a widespread notion among violinists: A violin "opens up" as it is played, which is to say its sound gradually improves. However, an experiment conducted by a team led by a CNRS researcher has challenged this belief in a study published in Acta Acustica. After six months, the professional soloist in charge of playing the violin judged the process complete, reporting that the instrument had become easier to play and its tone had improved. Yet, no physical or acoustic measurement confirmed that this feeling resulted from such a mechanical change in the instrument itself.

phys.org/news/2026-11-genetic-mosaic-div.title: Genetic mosaic helps explain diverse forms of Darwin's finches
phys.org/news/2026-11-genetic-mosaic-div.excerpt: Darwin's finches are known for their varied beaks, which help them take advantage of different food sources in the Galápagos Islands. Much previous research has focused on seed-eating ground finches, but their relatives that search for insects in forested areas have received less attention.

phys.org/news/2026-11-recipe-world-impor.title: Recipe for one of the world's most important cancer drugs uncovered: Tobacco plants could produce the medicine
phys.org/news/2026-11-recipe-world-impor.excerpt: More people around the world will receive a cancer diagnosis at some point in their lives. As this trend is expected to continue, researchers have been working to crack the code of how the widely used cancer drug Taxol (paclitaxel) is naturally produced, with the aim of making its production cheaper and more efficient in the future.

phys.org/news/2026-11-local-reveal-globa.title: Local measurements reveal global quantum properties in a constant number of experimental runs
phys.org/news/2026-11-local-reveal-globa.excerpt: A quantum device with more qubits is harder to verify. Describing a general quantum state takes an exponential number of parameters, and reconstructing it in full—a procedure known as state tomography—becomes impractical as the system grows. Yet most experiments do not need the full description. They need to know a few things: Is the state close to the target? Are the qubits entangled? And does the system carry the resources needed for quantum computation?

phys.org/news/2026-11-electron-microscop.title: Electron microscopy reveals the headquarters of poxviruses
phys.org/news/2026-11-electron-microscop.excerpt: Mpox remains a smoldering threat, with recent clusters in Brazil, Thailand and Austria and ongoing hot spots across multiple African countries. Other poxviruses also endanger human or animal health. A new study by the Institute of Science and Technology Austria (ISTA) uncovers the inner workings of the poxvirus core: how its gene-copying machines sit parked in dormant pairs, ready to print viral instructions and release them into the host cell through dedicated export portals embedded in the core shell.

phys.org/news/2026-11-consumers-obliviou.title: Consumers, oblivious of being targeted, find online ads helpful
phys.org/news/2026-11-consumers-obliviou.excerpt: Most online shoppers know that ads strategically follow them across sites, a mechanism known as "ad retargeting." A new study led by Penn State researchers found that consumers find these targeted ads helpful, but explaining why they are seeing an ad can backfire by increasing concerns about being watched.

phys.org/news/2026-11-nasa-spacecraft-re.title: NASA spacecraft data reveal how solar system's tail shifts over 14 years
phys.org/news/2026-11-nasa-spacecraft-re.excerpt: A Southwest Research Institute-led study is the first to map out the distinct motion paths of the heliotail lobes across a 14-year period using data from NASA's Interstellar Boundary Explorer (IBEX) spacecraft. By identifying the paths followed by these lobes, the study provides a better understanding of how solar activity shapes the heliotail.

phys.org/news/2026-11-physics-ai-reconst.title: Physics-guided AI reconstructs fluid flow from sparse, noisy data
phys.org/news/2026-11-physics-ai-reconst.excerpt: Medical imaging technologies have transformed how scientists and physicians visualize blood flowing through the human heart, but even the most advanced imaging techniques cannot capture every detail of fluid motion. Researchers at the University of California, Irvine, have developed a computational approach that combines fundamental physics with artificial intelligence to reconstruct a more complete and accurate picture of fluid flow from limited and imperfect measurements.

phys.org/news/2026-11-million-year-hairy.title: A nearly 100-million-year-old hairy snail pays tribute to the Prodigy's lead singer
phys.org/news/2026-11-million-year-hairy.excerpt: Myanmar amber (more commonly known as "burmite") is one of the most important sources of information about biodiversity during the Mesozoic Era. This amber dates back to the age of the dinosaurs and is approximately 99 million years old. Burmite preserves numerous now-extinct organisms (animals, plants, fungi, etc.) as inclusions, often in astonishing detail. This is because amber can preserve even soft tissues, which would otherwise decompose rapidly, and do so in three dimensions.

phys.org/news/2026-11-cactus-gears-pear..title: A cactus that changes gears: How the prickly pear makes the most of desert rain
phys.org/news/2026-11-cactus-gears-pear..excerpt: In the desert, water doesn't arrive steadily. It comes in short pulses: a winter storm, a few rainy days, then months of drought. A desert plant needs two skills to live there. It has to survive the long dry spells, and it has to make full use of the brief windows when water is plentiful. A new study from Ben-Gurion University of the Negev and the Volcani Institute shows that the prickly pear cactus has an unexpected way of doing both.

phys.org/news/2026-11-overlooked-symmetr.title: Overlooked symmetry group offers new geometric blueprint for the Standard Model and topologically protected vacuums
phys.org/news/2026-11-overlooked-symmetr.excerpt: For more than half a century, physicists searching for a grand unified theory have followed one unspoken rule: go bigger. If you want to weave nature's fundamental forces into a single mathematical framework, the classic recipe says you need a giant "simple" symmetry group—structures like SU(5) or SO(10) that act like massive algebraic warehouses large enough to hold every force at once.

phys.org/news/2026-11-hidden-link-scent-.title: A hidden link between a flower's color and its scent revealed
phys.org/news/2026-11-hidden-link-scent-.excerpt: Researchers discovered that the biological machinery behind flower color also helps shape fragrance. By disrupting a single gene in petunias, they changed the flowers' mix of scent compounds, increasing some associated with vanilla and cloves.

phys.org/news/2026-11-south-africa-small.title: South Africa's small cattle farmers need help before super El Niño hits: How to set up shade, water and feed
phys.org/news/2026-11-south-africa-small.excerpt: In South Africa, more than 2 million smallholder households make a living through agriculture. Within this small-scale farming sector, roughly 613,000 families own cattle. They farm on shared rural rangelands.

phys.org/news/2026-11-nanoparticles-mito.title: Nanoparticles repair mitochondria to boost bone regeneration in diabetic rats
phys.org/news/2026-11-nanoparticles-mito.excerpt: A complication of diabetes is that damaged bones don't heal well, but a group of researchers is helping solve the problem with a novel mechanism to help bone regeneration.

phys.org/news/2026-11-webb-evidence-star.title: Webb finds evidence star's layers may have merged just hours before Cas A supernova
phys.org/news/2026-11-webb-evidence-star.excerpt: NASA's James Webb Space Telescope has painted a vibrant tapestry of the legendary supernova remnant Cassiopeia A (Cas A). Remnants like these are the clouds of gas and dust that remain following the explosion of a massive star and will eventually seed a new generation of stars and planets.

phys.org/news/2026-11-hera-surveys-aster.excerpt: The European Space Agency's Hera mission for planetary defense surveys its target asteroids with a combination of instruments, peering beyond the limits of the human eye. The larger Didymos asteroid—dominated by its dramatic equatorial ridge—is seen here from just 28.5 km (17.7 miles) away, variously in visible light, multispectral and thermal infrared vision.

phys.org/news/2026-11-center-policy-reve.title: Data center policy review reveals 'chaotic' patchwork of rules across all 50 states
phys.org/news/2026-11-center-policy-reve.excerpt: The artificial intelligence boom has brought with it debates about where the data centers that run the technology will be located, how big they will be and how to ensure communities benefit from them. Underlying these debates is the question of whether state and local governments should ban them outright, welcome them with open arms or choose something in between.

phys.org/news/2026-11-satellite-earth-na.title: Satellite observations show how rain breaks up Earth's natural sunshades
phys.org/news/2026-11-satellite-earth-na.excerpt: Delivering on its promise, the European Space Agency's EarthCARE satellite is already yielding new insights into the role that clouds play in regulating Earth's climate. The latest findings shed light on one of the processes that leads to the breakup of vast, bright cloud formations that help keep our planet cool—with rain emerging as a key driver.

phys.org/news/2026-11-people-languages-p.title: Some people claim to speak many languages. But what does it really mean to be a polyglot?
phys.org/news/2026-11-people-languages-p.excerpt: Roughly half of the world's population speaks more than one language. But speaking two or three languages is very different from claiming proficiency in five, 10 or more.

phys.org/news/2026-11-reparations-ground.title: Reparations can work when claims are grounded in solid evidence
phys.org/news/2026-11-reparations-ground.excerpt: At the Commonwealth summit in Antigua in November 2026, Britain's King Charles expressed sorrow for Britain's role in the slave trade.

phys.org/news/2026-11-stellar-pulses-rev.title: Stellar pulses reveal hidden binary in JWST calibration star sample
phys.org/news/2026-11-stellar-pulses-rev.excerpt: Stars used to calibrate the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) must have precisely characterized spectra so that their fluxes can be measured accurately. Yet some stars that appear single may in fact harbor unresolved companions that alter their predicted radiation. One such object, HD 158485—an A-type star in the JWST calibration program—has now been shown to be a binary system whose two stars both pulsate.

phys.org/news/2026-11-pollen-honey-autom.title: Which pollen is found in honey? Automated analysis closely matches conventional testing
phys.org/news/2026-11-pollen-honey-autom.excerpt: Pure rapeseed honey—or not quite? Single-flower honeys must contain a certain proportion of pollen from the respective plant. This is assessed by pollen analysis, which is time-consuming and requires specialist expertise. As part of a collaborative project, a research team from the Helmholtz Centre for Environmental Research (UFZ) and the German Centre for Integrative Biodiversity Research (iDiv) in Leipzig worked with several partners to develop an automated, AI-based pollen analysis method for honey testing.

phys.org/news/2026-11-discovery-curse-ri.title: Discovery of curse ritual in trash dump surprises Egyptologist: 'It must have been widespread in ancient Egypt'
phys.org/news/2026-11-discovery-curse-ri.excerpt: The discovery of 40 charred papyrus fragments at a temple in the ancient city of Thebes is changing researchers' understanding of one of ancient Egypt's most famous curse rituals. The fragments show that the ritual was probably far more widespread and commonplace than previously believed.

livescience.com/planet-earth/volcanoes/g.title: Growing lava dome oozes ‘like toothpaste’ from superactive snow-covered volcano in Russia
livescience.com/planet-earth/volcanoes/g.excerpt: A recent satellite image captured a striking scene at the Shiveluch volcano, which has been erupting for nearly 30 years in Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula.

livescience.com/space/bepicolombo-spacec.title: BepiColombo ends 8-year interplanetary journey to Mercury. What's next for the ambitious spacecraft?

universetoday.com/articles/space-lasers-.excerpt: Since the launch of Sputnik, humanity has talked to its spacecraft through radio waves. Radio is great for communication through any weather, but it has hit a limit – traditional radio frequencies are highly regulated by bodies like the International Telecommunications Union, which limits the scalability of radio communications networks to meet the growing demand of bandwidth to and from space. The obvious solution is to switch to infrared lasers, which have an extremely high data transfer rate. However, according to a paper available in pre-print on arXiv from Dr. Slava Turyshev – best known to UT readers for his work on turning the Sun’s gravity into a giant telescope – the raw speed of laser communication isn’t the bottleneck, it’s the system’s reliability.

phys.org/news/2026-11-simulations-reveal.excerpt: Solar spicules are slender jets commonly found in the chromosphere. They lift relatively cool plasma from the lower solar atmosphere, carry energy upward, and in some cases rotate as they evolve. Small-scale vortices also occur frequently between convection-driven granules in the photosphere. Two questions remain incompletely answered: how these photospheric vortices help form spicules, and how much mass and energy the rising jets carry into the corona.

phys.org/news/2026-11-marine-life-atmosp.title: Without marine life, atmospheric CO₂ would shoot up by up to 65% by the end of the century
phys.org/news/2026-11-marine-life-atmosp.excerpt: Without marine organisms transporting carbon into the deep ocean, the accumulation of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere would be drastically higher in the year 2100, reaching levels between 35% and 65% higher than projected. This is one of the main conclusions of the new policy brief developed within the framework of the European OceanICU project, which was presented at the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Türkiye.

phys.org/news/2026-11-agility-2d-crystal.title: Structural agility of 2D crystals enables digital doping of graphene superlattices
phys.org/news/2026-11-agility-2d-crystal.excerpt: A study published in Nature has demonstrated that applying an electric field can switch the atomic arrangement in a stack of two-dimensional (2D) crystals, accompanied by an unusual charge behavior. This provides a new experimental platform for exploring how the structural and electronic properties of atomically thin materials interact.

phys.org/news/2026-11-uterine-pressure-t.title: Uterine pressure guides head-to-tail axis formation in mouse embryos
phys.org/news/2026-11-uterine-pressure-t.excerpt: During animal development, the establishment of the three primary body axes—head-to-tail (anterior-posterior), dorsal-ventral and left-right—is essential for building a proper body structure. A fertilized egg, initially a single cell, undergoes repeated cell divisions to form a multicellular structure called an embryo, and body axes are formed within the embryo.

phys.org/news/2026-11-weak-oversight-fin.title: Weak oversight and financial incentives may fuel health care corruption, review finds
phys.org/news/2026-11-weak-oversight-fin.excerpt: Corruption in health systems may arise when governance failures offer opportunities and systemic vulnerabilities provide incentives for private gain, according to an umbrella review published in the open-access journal PLOS Global Public Health by Michele Coleman and Petra Varkonyi from the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, United Kingdom, and colleagues.

phys.org/news/2026-11-triple-helix-rare-.title: The triple helix: How a rare twist in human evolution may influence fetal cooling
phys.org/news/2026-11-triple-helix-rare-.excerpt: The human umbilical cord is an evolutionary rarity, with the arrangement of blood vessels within its distinctive twisted structure potentially helping unborn babies stay cool in the womb, according to a team led by University of Manchester and University of Southampton scientists.

phys.org/news/2026-11-uncharted-plate-te.title: Mapping the uncharted plate tectonic cycle: The hidden path from plate destruction to new oceanic crust
phys.org/news/2026-11-uncharted-plate-te.excerpt: Since the discovery of plate tectonics, the ultimate fate of the massive plates that sink into Earth's interior mantle at subduction zones has remained a major geological quest. Meanwhile, magma continuously rises from the deep mantle to form new oceanic crust, erupting as mid-ocean ridge basalts (MORB).

phys.org/news/2026-11-england-summer-thu.title: New England's summer thunderstorms grow shorter and heavier, raising flash flood risk
phys.org/news/2026-11-england-summer-thu.excerpt: A growing share of New England's summer rain is falling in the form of heavy, heat-related showers and thunderstorms, raising the risk of flash flooding events across the region as the climate continues to warm. That's according to a new study by Brown University researchers published in Science Advances.

phys.org/news/2026-11-errors-friendships.title: Errors in judging friendships predict who will connect or drift apart six months later
phys.org/news/2026-11-errors-friendships.excerpt: Decades of research show that mental representations of social networks are riddled with errors, with people commonly misidentifying existing ties and reporting relationships that do not exist. While these inaccuracies have been interpreted as noise arising from the limits of memory or attention, Brown University researchers have discovered a much more intriguing explanation: These "errors" are accurate representations of social connections that just haven't happened yet.

phys.org/news/2026-11-evolution-genes-sy.title: Evolution's balancing act—keeping genes in sync after genome duplication
phys.org/news/2026-11-evolution-genes-sy.excerpt: Getting the right balance is important in all walks of life, whether it's a healthy combination of food groups in a balanced diet or a balanced mix of skills that allows a work or sports team to succeed.

phys.org/news/2026-11-birds-seabirds-rev.title: The birds are listening: Seabirds reveal hidden fishing activity at sea
phys.org/news/2026-11-birds-seabirds-rev.excerpt: Researchers from the University of Oxford fitted miniature audio recorders and GPS trackers to seabirds to better understand the impacts of fishing boats on wildlife. This revealed that seabirds may be interacting with human vessels considerably more than official tracking data suggest. The results have been published on Nov. 25 in Science Advances.

phys.org/news/2026-11-antidiscrimination.title: Antidiscrimination laws in US often lack clear wording relevant to multiracial identities
phys.org/news/2026-11-antidiscrimination.excerpt: A new analysis highlights the limited appearance of the phrases "perceived race" and "multiracial" in U.S. federal and state antidiscrimination laws and demonstrates how court cases can be analyzed to explore whether such wording contributes to ambiguity that may hamper equal protection of multiracial people. Victoria Jackson and colleagues at Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health, U.S., present these findings in the journal PLOS One on Nov. 25, 2026.

phys.org/news/2026-11-global-ocean-iodin.title: Global ocean iodine won't offset future air pollution, study warns
phys.org/news/2026-11-global-ocean-iodin.excerpt: The world's oceans will not play the role of scrubbing harmful ozone pollution from the atmosphere as the planet warms in the way that was expected, new research suggests.

phys.org/news/2026-11-nasa-hubble-views-.excerpt: An expanse of stars gleams in a rainbow of colors in these NASA Hubble Space Telescope images of the Milky Way. The images focus on an area of sky toward the galactic bulge, a densely packed, spherical region of stars that surrounds the center of a galaxy's disk. These Hubble observations are part of a survey that will help researchers better interpret upcoming Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope observations as they seek to characterize the stars and search for exoplanets in this busy region of our galaxy.

phys.org/news/2026-11-ancient-cahokia-dr.title: Ancient Cahokia transformed amid droughts and flooding—climate change is reshaping modern communities in similar ways
phys.org/news/2026-11-ancient-cahokia-dr.excerpt: More than 800 years ago, a combination of environmental and societal challenges led some Mississippian people to leave Cahokia, a massive archaeological site that was once home to 20,000 people near modern-day St. Louis. Just south of Cahokia, another archaeological site is taking shape at Centreville, Illinois, as modern-day people abandon their homes in the face of 21st-century climate and cultural changes.

phys.org/news/2026-11-kazakhstan-endemic.title: Only one in five of Kazakhstan's endemic plants has data for initial range screening
phys.org/news/2026-11-kazakhstan-endemic.excerpt: Kazakhstan has hundreds of plant species found nowhere else in the world. Many have been known to botanists for decades, described in floristic publications and held in herbarium collections. Yet knowing that a plant exists is different from having the information needed to judge its prospects for survival.

phys.org/news/2026-11-cells-adjust-gene-.title: Cells can adjust gene activity to partly offset extra or missing chromosomes
phys.org/news/2026-11-cells-adjust-gene-.excerpt: When a cell loses or gains an extra chromosome, the activity of hundreds or even thousands of genes is affected. A new study published in Nature Communications shows that cells have a much greater ability than previously thought to compensate for such changes. The findings provide new insight into how genes are regulated and may help improve our understanding of how cancer cells cope with major changes in their genetic material.

phys.org/news/2026-11-quantum-network-en.title: New quantum network entangles 123 qubits that store information in atoms' positions
phys.org/news/2026-11-quantum-network-en.excerpt: Researchers are constantly getting closer to making practical quantum computers. phys.org/news/2026-11-rubik-cube-molecul.excerpt: Plastics that are both good at conducting electricity and flexible enough to stretch and bend are already being used in cell phones with folding screens. But because the rigid crystals they contain—which help with conductivity—aren't naturally flexible, they still often crack. Now, researchers from the University of Toronto have found a way to increase the stretchiness of these materials while maintaining their ability to conduct electricity, potentially opening new uses in medicine and biology.

phys.org/news/2026-11-mountain-gorillas-.title: Mountain gorillas that survive early hardship show few signs of lasting social isolation
phys.org/news/2026-11-mountain-gorillas-.excerpt: In Rwanda's Volcanoes National Park, researchers found little sign that losing a parent, growing up with few companions of the same age or facing other early hardships left surviving mountain gorillas socially isolated. Males that had experienced more types of hardship before age 6 later spent more time near other males than their peers that had fewer such experiences. Among females still living in their birth groups, those that faced more hardships also spent more time near other females.

phys.org/news/2026-11-workplace-reveal-p.title: Workplace connections reveal a quitting paradox: Too few or too many may increase risk
phys.org/news/2026-11-workplace-reveal-p.excerpt: Being the one everyone turns to at work may seem like a privileged position. You know the right people, receive important information and take part in decisions. But there is a hidden cost: messages pile up, requests keep coming, meetings overlap and concentrating on your own work becomes increasingly difficult. Eventually, paradoxically, the very people most involved in company life may begin to want to leave.

phys.org/news/2026-11-narwhals-vulnerabl.title: Narwhals may be most vulnerable in Arctic food fight over changing marine ecosystem
phys.org/news/2026-11-narwhals-vulnerabl.excerpt: Warming waters are changing the Arctic marine ecosystem, potentially leading to increased competition for food among seals and narwhals, according to a research team at the National Institute of Polar Research in Japan. The group compared diets of the only four marine mammals that inhabit the same fjord in Greenland each summer and found significant dietary overlap. Of the mammals, narwhals had the lowest dietary diversity compared to ringed seals, harp seals and bearded seals, suggesting they may be particularly vulnerable to marine ecosystem changes, the team said.

phys.org/news/2026-11-phosphate-boosts-n.excerpt: Nitrate is a major water pollutant, and remediation technologies like catalytic electrochemical reduction remove nitrate by converting it into other compounds. This complex chemical reaction has many end products, among which is ammonia. Ammonia has many uses in agriculture and chemistry, but it is difficult to obtain as an end product using a copper catalyst.

Unlike Wi-Fi or radio signals, gravity passes through ordinary barriers without being blocked, offering a potentially revolutionary way to communicate.

universetoday.com/articles/using-lunar-c.title: Using Lunar Craters as Free Radiation Shields for Moon Base Nuclear Reactors
universetoday.com/articles/using-lunar-c.excerpt: Powering any future lunar base is a massive engineering challenge. The two-week lunar night can drain batteries charged by solar panels during the two-week day, if the batteries themselves can even withstand the freezing temperatures that go along with it. So, for decades at this point, engineers have planned to use a nuclear reactor to at least partially power any future human settlement on the Moon. A new paper from researchers at Los Alamos, NASA Glenn, Oak Ridge, Idaho National Lab, and Lockheed Martin, and presented at the American Nuclear Society’s Nuclear and Emerging Technologies for Space (NETS) conference back in April, offers a simple solution to one major problem for any such future nuclear reactor - shielding.

universetoday.com/articles/comet-enckes-.title: Comet Encke's Shape and Heat Revealed in Thermal Glow

On Nov. 20, 2026, a mathematician at the AI company Anthropic claimed that while working with the model Claude, he had solved the generalized Riemann hypothesis, the most famous problem in mathematics. This problem has stood unsolved for 167 years, and solving it could easily warrant a Fields Medal—considered equivalent to a Nobel Prize, but for mathematics.

phys.org/news/2026-11-dinosaurs-tore-mea.title: Dinosaurs likely tore meat like birds of prey
phys.org/news/2026-11-dinosaurs-tore-mea.excerpt: Meat-eating dinosaurs probably fed by dragging their teeth backward through flesh like a saw rather than biting straight down like a dagger, new experiments suggest.

phys.org/news/2026-11-ai-doesnt-deter.ht.title: Disliking AI doesn't deter its influence
phys.org/news/2026-11-ai-doesnt-deter.ht.excerpt: An aversion to artificial intelligence (AI) does not lessen the influence of the technology on people and their decision-making, according to new research from City St George's, University of London.

phys.org/news/2026-11-sweden-tops-global.title: Sweden tops global media freedom support rankings as international funding declines
phys.org/news/2026-11-sweden-tops-global.excerpt: Sweden has been ranked the world's leading supporter of international media freedom, according to a new index. The index also highlights a decline in funding from 30 leading donor countries, despite growing threats to independent journalism worldwide.

phys.org/news/2026-11-giant-deer-bones-h.title: Giant deer bones may push human arrival in Ireland back by 1,000 years
phys.org/news/2026-11-giant-deer-bones-h.excerpt: A team of archaeologists and scientists has uncovered tantalizing new evidence that Late Upper Paleolithic hunter-gatherers may have lived in southern Ireland around 13,500 years ago—nearly a millennium earlier than currently confirmed.

phys.org/news/2026-11-fermented-held-rit.title: Fermented milk may have held ritual power in Neolithic Denmark
phys.org/news/2026-11-fermented-held-rit.excerpt: Experimental archaeology sheds light on the substances fermented in Neolithic Scandinavian pottery and deposited in tombs, suggesting fermented dairy products held symbolic significance in prehistoric funerary rituals.

phys.org/news/2026-11-minecraft-dna-cube.title: Minecraft-like DNA cubes self-assemble into complex 3D nanostructures
phys.org/news/2026-11-minecraft-dna-cube.excerpt: Associate professor Petr Sulc and his research team have developed a programmable DNA-based building system that could open new possibilities for nanorobots, three-dimensional electronics and next-generation nanotechnology.

phys.org/news/2026-11-artificial-photosy.title: Artificial photosynthesis uses waste CO₂ to grow protein-rich edible fungus in seven days
phys.org/news/2026-11-artificial-photosy.excerpt: While many people think first of meat when they think about dietary protein, most protein ultimately depends on plants, since livestock feed on grass, hay and other plants. Meeting the demand for protein is taxing on the environment, requiring massive amounts of land and water while creating greenhouse gas emissions. And that demand is expected to require nearly 50% more agricultural production by 2050 than in 2012, according to the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organization.

phys.org/news/2026-11-peatlands-legacy.h.title: Draining peatlands leaves a long legacy of warming
phys.org/news/2026-11-peatlands-legacy.h.excerpt: Peatland ecosystems like bogs and swamps perform an important balancing act: Their vegetation takes up huge amounts of carbon dioxide, while their soil microbes produce methane. Although methane is a potent greenhouse gas, peatlands exhibit a net cooling effect on the planet because of the sheer scale of carbon dioxide they remove from the atmosphere, which has amounted to hundreds of gigatons globally over thousands of years.

phys.org/news/2026-11-stabilizing-atomic.title: Stabilizing atomically thin metals with sandwich structures: Machine learning expands the search
phys.org/news/2026-11-stabilizing-atomic.excerpt: Atomically thin metals, metallenes, are promising materials for catalysis, electronics and energy conversion, but their synthesis has been challenging. Researchers from the University of Jyväskylä have now identified more than 300 stable metallene sandwich structures using machine learning and high-performance computing. The results provide researchers with a practical roadmap for the fabrication of new two-dimensional metals.

phys.org/news/2026-11-smartphone-app-ai-.title: Smartphone app uses AI to identify illegal wildlife products
phys.org/news/2026-11-smartphone-app-ai-.excerpt: Illegal and unsustainable wildlife trade is a major driver of biodiversity loss. Thousands of animal species are traded, along with products made from them, ranging from ivory to scales and powders.

phys.org/news/2026-11-fungi-specialized-.title: Certain fungi turn specialized plant cells into water-carrying cells using one protein
phys.org/news/2026-11-fungi-specialized-.excerpt: Can a pathogen that causes damage to a plant also make that plant more resilient to drought? An international research team led by the University of Göttingen has investigated this apparent paradox. The researchers discovered how certain fungi promote the formation of new water-conducting cells in plants. At the same time, infected plants showed increased tolerance to drought stress. The results were published in the journal Cell Host & Microbe.

phys.org/news/2026-11-carbon-nanotube-re.title: Carbon nanotube measurements reveal quantum model better explains collective electron behavior
phys.org/news/2026-11-carbon-nanotube-re.excerpt: An international team of scientists from Lithuania, Finland and Israel has conducted both theoretical and experimental research into carbon nanotubes, becoming the first to demonstrate which physical model governs the motion and interactions of electrons within them.

phys.org/news/2026-11-five-reasons-why-w.title: Five reasons why we should still make things with our hands
phys.org/news/2026-11-five-reasons-why-w.excerpt: It's 7 a.m. Still dark outside. "Alex, time to wake up! You have a busy day ahead, with an important meeting at 8:30," announces the alarm in a soft but firm voice. Alex wakes up immediately, already thinking about the presentation that still needs a few finishing touches. In the kitchen, the coffee machine, set up for 7 a.m. sharp, has just finished brewing. "Alexa, set the temperature to 20 degrees," says Alex, reaching for the coffee.

phys.org/news/2026-11-inhibitor-antibiot.title: New inhibitor restores antibiotic activity against drug-resistant bacteria
phys.org/news/2026-11-inhibitor-antibiot.excerpt: Researchers from Imperial College London and collaborators have identified a potent small-molecule inhibitor that can restore the activity of the antibiotic ciprofloxacin against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA).

phys.org/news/2026-11-nasa-europa-clippe.title: NASA's Europa Clipper zooming by Earth on way to Jupiter's icy moon
phys.org/news/2026-11-nasa-europa-clippe.excerpt: NASA's Europa Clipper will soon swing past Earth before making a yearslong beeline for Jupiter, where the orbiter will probe whether the ocean beneath its moon Europa's icy shell has the ingredients for life. The flyby will offer a propellant-saving boost and an opportunity to prepare for the science-gathering that lies ahead.

phys.org/news/2026-11-collector-buy.html.title: Shopping as a 'collector' makes us want to buy more, new research shows
phys.org/news/2026-11-collector-buy.html.excerpt: Shoppers are more likely to buy products and pay more for them when they adopt a "collecting mindset," according to new research co-authored by Bayes Business School (City St George's, University of London).

phys.org/news/2026-11-giant-lambda-stell.title: Giant lambda-shaped stellar nursery found in the Milky Way's outskirts
phys.org/news/2026-11-giant-lambda-stell.excerpt: Massive stars often form in dense regions, called "hubs," where filamentary structures made of star-forming materials meet. These star-forming complexes are "hub-filament" systems. Astronomers have discovered one such large network of molecular gas filaments in the outer regions of the Milky Way. It is called the λ-complex, and the structure is bigger than most known hub-filament systems. The research paper was published in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society on Nov. 17.

phys.org/news/2026-11-sustainable-multin.title: Sustainable procurement in multinational corporations depends on people and the operating environment
phys.org/news/2026-11-sustainable-multin.excerpt: Elizabeth Jeromaa's doctoral dissertation in management, to be examined at the University of Vaasa, demonstrates that it is possible for companies to implement environmentally sustainable procurement practices, though there is no one-size-fits-all model.

phys.org/news/2026-11-heaven-scent-link-.title: Heaven scent: Study shows link between a partner's body odor and sexual intimacy
phys.org/news/2026-11-heaven-scent-link-.excerpt: Many people spend a considerable amount of time and money trying to disguise their natural body odor. But not everyone finds our natural scent unpleasant. In fact, it could be part of what makes a couple click.

phys.org/news/2026-11-lunar-craters-free.title: Using lunar craters as free radiation shields for moon base nuclear reactors
phys.org/news/2026-11-lunar-craters-free.excerpt: Powering any future lunar base is a massive engineering challenge. The two-week lunar night can drain batteries charged by solar panels during the two-week day, if the batteries themselves can even withstand the freezing temperatures that go along with it. So, for decades at this point, engineers have planned to use a nuclear reactor to at least partially power any future human settlement on the moon.

sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261125.title: Scientists discover mysterious lakes more than a mile beneath the Red Sea
sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261125.excerpt: More than a mile beneath the surface of the Red Sea, scientists have discovered rare underwater lakes that could reveal secrets about Earth's ancient oceans and the possibility of alien life. Known as brine pools, these extremely salty, oxygen-free environments are surprisingly teeming with microbial life, challenging our understanding of where living organisms can survive.

sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261122.excerpt: A mysterious object named Phoebe, detected when it briefly magnified a distant star, could be a primordial black hole formed just after the Big Bang. With an estimated mass only three times that of the Moon, it may be a 13-billion-year-old cosmic relic that offers new clues to the mystery of dark matter.

arxiv.org/abs/2611.33214.title: OSIRIS-REx Lessons Learned Report: Insights from the Journey to Bennu and Back
arxiv.org/abs/2611.33214.excerpt:
arXiv:2611.33214v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: OSIRIS-REx, NASA's third New Frontiers mission, was the first U.S. mission to return a sample from an asteroid. Proposed in 2010 for an \$811 million lifecycle cost, the mission was completed for \$828 million, returned more than \$52 million of Headquarters reserves unused, and delivered at least 121.6 g of pristine material from near-Earth asteroid (101955) Bennu in September 2023, more than twice the Level-1 requirement. It did so despite a surface far more rugged than predicted, the discovery of particle ejection, sampling in a regolith much weaker than expected, operations during the COVID-19 pandemic, and an off-nominal parachute sequence on Earth return. This report sets out the lessons learned by the mission's leadership across six areas: leadership and governance; cost, schedule and risk management; systems engineering; mission operations; sample return, curation and analysis; and data archiving. Recurring themes are that a PI-led structure integrating science, engineering and project management gives the discipline to make fast, informed decisions; that reserves and schedule margin spent early to retire risk, such as funding Natural Feature Tracking as a backup navigation system, buy the flexibility to absorb discovery; that heritage hardware reduces risk only when its verification and engineering knowledge are preserved; and that contamination knowledge, sample science and data stewardship are mission-long responsibilities, not post-flight tasks. Each section pairs background with specific recommendations for future sample-return and small-body missions.

arxiv.org/abs/2611.33215.title: Modeling the LISA response in the time-frequency domain
arxiv.org/abs/2611.33215.excerpt:
arXiv:2611.33215v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Time-frequency methods are a promising approach to LISA data analysis. This paper presents a model for the LISA response directly in the time-frequency domain using the Wilson-Daubechies-Meyer (WDM) transformation. The implementation is vectorized using JAX and can efficiently evaluate the response for batches of signals, achieving white-noise mismatches of $\sim 10^{-9}$ compared to existing implementations of the LISA one-arm response. Our results demonstrate that the LISA response can be modeled accurately and efficiently in the time-frequency domain, providing an important component of an end-to-end time-frequency LISA analysis framework.

arxiv.org/abs/2611.33239.title: RIFT for the O4 era: operating points, calibration marginalization, and cross-code validation
arxiv.org/abs/2611.33239.excerpt:
arXiv:2611.33239v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The Rapid Iterative FiTting (RIFT) parameter inference algorithm provides a simulation-based-inference approach to efficient, highly-parallelized parameter inference for GW sources. In this paper, we describe improvements deployed during preparations for and analysis of O4 observations (versions 0.0.17.3--0.0.18.0) that broaden RIFT's reach for single-event inference with contemporary instruments. We provide additional options to increase compatibility and comparability with other codes, notably including (a) enhancing RIFT's capabilities for calibration marginalization; (b) managing our likelihood's internal, output, and time-interpolated representation; (c) introducing new coordinates for (transverse) spin and eccentric mean anomaly, enabling more robust inference of parameters with subtle and complex correlations to others, and (d) revised operating point choices better suited to the loudest, clearest signals. We identify and reconcile the most substantial sources of head-to-head likelihood differences between RIFT and other production inference codes, and describe automated waveform symmetry checks that detect upstream model regressions before they bias inference. Using the previously-reported RIFT/asimov interface for reproducible settings consistent with past work, we demonstrate these capabilities end to end.

arxiv.org/abs/2611.33269.title: RR Lyrae stars as distance indicators I. Sample selection and characterisation
arxiv.org/abs/2611.33269.excerpt:
arXiv:2611.33269v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: RR Lyrae stars (RRL) are well-established Population II distance indicators, with period-metallicity-luminosity (PLZ) relations linking pulsational properties to absolute luminosity. Gaia parallaxes now allow these relations to be anchored to geometric distances with unprecedented precision, offering an independent route to the extragalactic distance scale. We present the first paper in a series aimed at deriving new empirical PLZ and metallicity-luminosity relations for RRL in the optical and near-infrared. We describe the selection and characterisation of a sample of bright nearby field RRL, with distances anchored to reliable Gaia DR3 parallaxes. We conducted a multi-band photometric campaign of 172 RRL: 101 in Johnson-Cousins UBVRI with the IAC80 telescope and 130 in JHKs with the IRSF telescope, with 59 stars in common. The iron abundances come from the Spectroscopic Rome RRL Catalog catalogue, mostly from high-resolution spectroscopy. The light curves were modelled with GLOESS (optical) and near-infrared templates, and the mean magnitudes, amplitudes, and Fourier parameters were derived via a bootstrap Monte Carlo method. The linear relations were fitted with a Bayesian Markov Chain Monte Carlo method. The sample spans -3.4 to 0.2 dex in [Fe/H]. We found tight relations between the Fourier parameter $\phi_{31}$ in each optical and Gaia band and its V-band value for RRab stars (scatter below 0.06). The near-infrared amplitude ratios with respect to V or G increase continuously with period, without the break reported in globular clusters. We provide a homogeneous calibration of the colour at minimum light across all filter combinations from U-B to H-Ks, revealing significant period and metallicity dependences, and we use it to derive reddening estimates for 15 stars outside current 3D extinction maps.

arxiv.org/abs/2611.33276.title: Constraining Intergalactic Dust with Supernova Color Evolution: Current Constraints from DES and Forecasts for LSST and Roman
arxiv.org/abs/2611.33276.excerpt:
arXiv:2611.33276v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Dust is an important systematic in precision Type Ia supernova (SN Ia) cosmology, and while dust in the Milky Way and SN host galaxies has been extensively studied, the impact of potential intergalactic dust is less well constrained. Using estimates from B. M\'enard et al. (2010), we find that current intergalactic dust bounds could shift SN distance moduli by up to 0.02 mag at $z \gtrsim 1$ from simulations. However, we show dust models can be constrained independently by SN samples themselves via a specific predicted redshift-dependent evolution observed in SN colors. While current data from the Dark Energy Survey (DES) cannot distinguish between various amounts of intergalactic dust in our universe, we demonstrate that the Roman Space Telescope (Roman) will place a significant constraint on intergalactic dust models ($>$ 3$\sigma$). In contrast, the Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), even with its unprecedented statistics, will only reach $\lesssim$ 2$\sigma$ significance on any given intergalactic dust prediction relative to no dust. We propagate multiple parameterizations of intergalactic dust through to cosmology. For LSST, we see a $\sim$60% reduction in the figure of merit (FoM) for $w$CDM and a $\sim$20% reduction for $w_0w_a$CDM, and for Roman, a $\sim$20% reduction in the FoM for $w$CDM and a $\sim$5% reduction for $w_0w_a$CDM. Utilizing Roman as an external constraint on dust for LSST results in a slightly improved FoM ($\sim$50% reduction) for $w$CDM for LSST. Finally, we show that intergalactic dust uncertainties decrease the FoM of the previous DES analysis (16.9% for $w$CDM and 8.1% for $w_0w_a$CDM) and that intergalactic dust cannot explain away recent hints for evolving dark energy.

arxiv.org/abs/2611.33282.title: When precision exceeds fidelity: systematic error quantification for inference with misspecified simulators
arxiv.org/abs/2611.33282.excerpt:
arXiv:2611.33282v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As scientific datasets grow in complexity and precision, the primary source of uncertainty in parameter inference shifts from measurement noise to systematic errors within the simulators themselves. In this setting, Bayesian evidence concentrates on whichever misspecified model best approximates the data. Evidence-weighted model averaging can then underestimate systematic uncertainty when one model component compensates for the misspecification of another component. We posit that in this case, the key question is how each model responds to discrepancies between simulator and data. We show that the local response of an inferred parameter to perturbations in the data --- the model's influence map --- can be estimated efficiently from forward evaluations of the simulator at existing posterior samples. Propagating discrepancy residuals through these influence maps enables individual sources of systematic bias to be isolated. Applied to independent observations used to infer the mass of a supermassive black hole, we find that the error is dominated by model systematics. We identify a simplification shared by all models, propagate the discrepancies through each model's influence map, and apply a first-order correction of the resulting biases. This substantially improves the cross-observation consistency of the inferred black-hole mass within each model while preserving the between-model spread that represents remaining systematics.

arxiv.org/abs/2611.33290.title: line racer: Rapid Calculation of Exoplanetary Radiative Opacities
arxiv.org/abs/2611.33290.excerpt:
arXiv:2611.33290v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Detailed studies of exoplanet and brown dwarf atmospheres rely on precise knowledge of the spectral features of possible atmospheric species. These features are a result of the interaction of different molecules and atoms with the radiation of the host star or the intrinsic thermal radiation of the object. The interaction is described by the opacity of a species, which determines how much light is absorbed at a given wavelength. The strength and shape of these opacities are very dependent on the temperature and pressure of the atmosphere, which is why they have to be calculated for a wide range of conditions. line racer is a Python package that enables computing high-resolution opacities from large molecular and atomic line lists in an effective manner. It offers users a wide range of options to customize opacity calculations to their needs and available hardware. The code is designed for efficient parallelization on multi-core and multi-node systems and can produce outputs compatible with popular atmospheric modeling and retrieval tools.

arxiv.org/abs/2611.33293.title: CHEX-MATE: Probing the thermal$-$non-thermal connection in radio halo clusters with LoTSS-DR2
arxiv.org/abs/2611.33293.excerpt:
arXiv:2611.33293v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The main baryonic component of galaxy clusters is in the form of a hot plasma observed in the X-rays. In addition, clusters host a non-thermal component (relativistic particles and magnetic fields) which is studied mainly via radio telescopes and is dynamically coupled to the thermal plasma. These two components evolve together within the system and are subject to both micro and macro-physical processes which can be traced only with deep and detailed observations. We present the first homogeneous spatially resolved radio--X-ray study of 18 radio halo clusters combining CHEX-MATE and the LOFAR Two metre Sky Survey DR2. Radio ($I_R$) and X-ray ($I_X$) surface brightness are clearly correlated (Spearman coefficient $r_s \ge 0.5$), following a typically sublinear $I_R-I_X$ relation ($67 \pm 5\%$ of the sample) that appears to be independent of other cluster properties, although a tentative trend with mass/redshift may be worth exploring with larger samples. When inspecting such a relation as a function of the radius, we observe a variety of behaviours, which suggest that the interplay between the thermal and non-thermal plasma components varies with radius. We find the averaged slope profile of dynamically disturbed clusters to be consistent with expectations from turbulent re-acceleration models where a constant ratio between cosmic-ray electron and thermal energy densities is assumed. Differently, less perturbed clusters require an increasing cosmic-ray-to-thermal energy ratio with radius. Finally, we show that radio halo surface-brightness profiles can be effectively rescaled using X-ray information and theoretical expectations. This procedure significantly reduces their scatter and reveals common underlying trends based on the cluster dynamics, resembling what is observed for the thermal ICM, and strengthening the idea of a strong interplay between these two plasma components.

arxiv.org/abs/2611.33297.title: The fate of Mercury's ejected mantle
arxiv.org/abs/2611.33297.excerpt:
arXiv:2611.33297v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Mercury's unusually high core mass fraction, inferred from its high bulk density, remains difficult to explain. Mantle stripping by a giant impact provides a plausible origin, but without efficient removal, the ejected debris remains on Mercury-crossing orbits and later gets re-accreted. Here, we show that re-accretion of impact debris onto Mercury is inefficient, making a giant-impact origin plausible. We combine N-body simulations of giant-impact ejecta with a collisional evolution model and consideration of processes acting on small dust. We find that, when the ejecta are dominated by large, several hundred km-sized non-vaporized fragments, the debris disk remains optically thin and the collisional cascade is truncated near the radiation-pressure blowout limit, where micron-sized grains are removed. In contrast, if vaporized, the ejecta recondense into mm to cm-sized droplets and form an optically thick disk, in which radiation pressure cannot efficiently truncate the cascade. The debris can then be ground down to nanometre-sized grains, where collisions become predominantly non-fragmenting and dissipative rather than destructive. Subsequent inelastic collisions damp the eccentricities and inclinations of the nanodust, producing a geometrically thin disk whose lifetime is governed by removal through exposed surface layers, where grains acquire large charge-to-mass ratios through solar UV radiation and are rapidly removed by electromagnetic forces. In either scenario, collisional evolution strongly reduces the re-accretion of debris and alleviates a key difficulty for the giant-impact origin of Mercury's large core. More broadly, highly energetic giant impacts in the inner regions of planetary systems may lead to short-lived populations of nanometre-sized dust.

arxiv.org/abs/2611.33301.title: Evidence for an Evolving Surface on the Partly Burnt Runaway Stellar Remnant GD 492
arxiv.org/abs/2611.33301.excerpt:
arXiv:2611.33301v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: GD 492 (LP 40-365) is a partly burnt, hypervelocity runaway stellar remnant thought to have survived a thermonuclear supernova. We analyze 12 sectors of TESS photometry spanning more than four years to investigate the previously reported 8.9-hr photometric modulation of the star. We find that the modulation changes with time, with individual-sector fits yielding apparent periods ranging from 8.8606 to 8.9048 hr (0.5% changes), more than 25 times the formal measurement uncertainties. Both the period and shape of the modulation evolve on a timescales of approximately one to two months. We show qualitatively that a two-spot model with evolving surface structure can reproduce several of the observed light-curve morphologies, although the geometry of the spots is not uniquely constrained. These observations suggest that changing surface inhomogeneities are a plausible origin of the photometric variability. Differential rotation and magnetic activity may contribute to this evolution, potentially providing new constraints on the outer convective structure of GD 492 and on the interpretation of its atmospheric abundances.

arxiv.org/abs/2611.33319.title: A Tale of Two Type IIb Supernovae: Radio-loud and Radio-silent Candidate Counterparts to Sub-solar Mass Gravitational-wave Triggers
arxiv.org/abs/2611.33319.excerpt:
arXiv:2611.33319v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: On 2025 November 12, the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA collaboration reported S251112cm, a gravitational-wave (GW) candidate from a compact binary merger with at least one sub-solar-mass component. Optical follow-up identified SN 2025adtq, a Type IIb supernova (SN) within the localization volume that exploded a few days before the merger. SN 2025adtq is the second Type IIb SN found to be potentially coincident with a sub-solar-mass GW candidate, after SN 2025ulz (S250818k). A key question is whether such SNe harbor fast, possibly collimated ejecta from a central engine, as invoked in ``superkilonova'' scenarios for forming sub-solar-mass neutron stars. We present deep Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array observations of SN 2025adtq from the JAGWAR program, spanning 139-216 days after the GW trigger at 6-10 GHz. The radio properties of SN 2025adtq differ substantially from those of SN 2025ulz: whereas SN 2025ulz has a significant 6-10 GHz counterpart, SN 2025adtq remains undetected to 3sigma limits of ~7.8 uJy, implying a radio luminosity density one order of magnitude below that of SN 2025ulz at a comparable epoch, excluding jet models that remained viable for SN 2025ulz. This diversity in radio properties calls for systematic multi-wavelength follow up observations of candidate sub-solar events in future runs of the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA detectors.

arxiv.org/abs/2611.33324.title: NuSrcAgent: An AI Agent for High-Energy Neutrino Source Searches
arxiv.org/abs/2611.33324.excerpt:
arXiv:2611.33324v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Identifying the sources of high-energy cosmic neutrinos is crucial for understanding cosmic particle accelerators and probing new physics. IceCube provides public data that allow researchers to search independently for neutrino sources, but these analyses require substantial technical expertise and careful scientific choices. We present \system, the first publicly available AI agent for high-energy neutrino source searches. Compared to public likelihood codes, \system is easier to install and use, and supports more analysis types. To start an analysis, users need only specify a source or catalog. The agent takes natural-language requests, runs likelihood analyses on public IceCube event data, and saves the settings and calculation records so users can repeat the analyses. We demonstrate \system through single-source and catalog stacking analyses, obtaining results consistent with IceCube results. These examples also show its ability to search the literature, analyze non-power-law spectra using user-provided model code, and develop new analysis functions, such as signal-injection simulations. \system is also a powerful tool for improving and testing existing analysis code, as we demonstrate by using it to refine the background probability density functions and reduce residuals and spurious signal contributions in stacking analyses. \system makes high-energy neutrino data analysis more accessible to the broader research community. Code and usage instructions: \href{https://github.com/beizhouphys/NuSrcAgent}{\faGithub\ {\tt github.com/beizhouphys/NuSrcAgent}}.

arxiv.org/abs/2611.33326.title: Beyond the blur: Radial binning trumps stellar migration in resolved star formation histories
arxiv.org/abs/2611.33326.excerpt:
arXiv:2611.33326v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Spatially resolved galaxy properties are routinely derived from integral-field spectroscopy and increasingly from multi-band photometry as a wealth of photometric data become available in large surveys like LSST/Rubin. Spatially resolved star formation histories (SFHs) offer a detailed view of galaxy growth and quenching by tracing the timing and location of star formation within a galaxy up to one billion years in the past. However, stellar migration between spaxels may strongly bias these reconstructions. Quantifying this bias remains challenging as few Milky-Way mass simulations fully resolve initial stellar dispersions or migration rates. We use the well-validated h277 Milky-Way-mass cosmological zoom simulation, which resolves both via explicitly tying star formation to the non-equilibrium abundance of H2, to assess the quality of specific star formation rates (sSFR) radial profiles inferred from resolved SFHs against actual values from stellar particle tracking. Across several evolutionary windows spanning a range of stellar activity stages from quiescent to star-bursting, we find that the adaptive radial binning imposed by S/N constraints in photometric SED fitting actually mitigates most of the blurring/mixing effects of stellar migration on inferred radial profiles up to lookback times of 1.5 Gyr. This allows for proper recovery of not only the average sSFR but also its radial slope, its relative changes in scatter across radial annuli and even approximate localization of low-z star-forming clumps. Only galaxies having undergone a major merger across the considered lookback time display discrepant, unreliable sSFR profiles, hence should not be considered for such reconstructions.

arxiv.org/abs/2611.33334.title: Acoustic Priors from the Latest Cosmic Microwave Background Data
arxiv.org/abs/2611.33334.excerpt:
arXiv:2611.33334v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We revisit the physics of the acoustic peaks and illustrate how early-Universe information in the cosmic microwave background (CMB) can be disentangled from late-time signatures imprinted by gravitational lensing and the integrated Sachs-Wolfe (ISW) effect. Applying this separation to Planck PR4, ACT DR6, and SPT-3G D1 temperature and polarization data combined with the joint lensing reconstruction, we update the model-independent constraints on the angular acoustic scale and the physical densities, $100\theta_*=1.04100\pm0.00021$, $\omega_{\rm b}=(2.2440\pm0.0099)\times10^{-2}$, and $\omega_{\rm bc}=0.1410\pm0.0011$. These constraints are consistent with the previous Planck PR4-only analysis and remain stable for extended late-time cosmologies beyond $\Lambda$CDM. Adding ACT DR6 to the combination favors a higher $\omega_{\rm b}$ and, through their correlation, a higher primordial tilt $n_{\rm s}$ than PR4 alone. The reconstructed lensing spectrum exceeds that of $\Lambda$CDM, with two features near $L\simeq50$ and $L\sim10^3$, and the excess is reduced when WMAP replaces the Planck primary spectra. Marginalizing over the lensing-induced peak smoothing, rather than tying it to the late-time model, lowers the preference of the CMB and DESI DR2 baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO) for $w_0w_a$CDM over $\Lambda$CDM from $3.0\sigma$ to $1.9\sigma$, or from $3.2\sigma$ to $2.4\sigma$ when Union3.1 supernovae are added. We further use the acoustic prior to predict BAO distances from CMB data alone under several late-time expansion histories, testing their consistency with DESI measurements assuming standard pre-recombination physics.

arxiv.org/abs/2611.33363.title: Toward Automated Strong-Lens Modeling with Agentic Workflows: An Application to Euclid Q1 Lenses
arxiv.org/abs/2611.33363.excerpt:
arXiv:2611.33363v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Ongoing and forthcoming wide-field surveys will discover $O(10^5)$ galaxy-galaxy strong lenses, shifting the main bottleneck from detection to reliable physical modeling. Conventional forward-modeling pipelines still rely on case-by-case expert judgment and manual tuning to mask contaminants, initialize priors, diagnose unphysical fits, and reconfigure failed runs. We present Lens-Orchestra, an automated workflow coupling a team of multimodal large language model agents to multi-stage physical modeling with elliptical power-law mass profiles, external shear, and pixelized source reconstructions. Launched via natural-language instructions, it modeled 185 Euclid Quick Data Release (Q1) grade-A lens candidates with published mass models without human intervention, completing 149 fits. Independent human evaluation confirmed 140 usable models, including 126 grade-I fits with noise-level residuals (with only 6.0% of completed fits unacceptable), and endorsed all 36 halted runs. Across the 140 usable systems, effective Einstein radii match released Q1 models (+0.12% median offset; 2.73% typical scatter), while hierarchical inference on the 126 grade-I imaging-only fits yields a mean mass-density slope of $2.002 \pm 0.009$ (intrinsic scatter $0.074^{+0.007}_{-0.006}$). A dedicated residual-screening agent also guided the selection of two candidate low-mass perturbers for parametric and free-form substructure modeling; although neither was confirmed, this end-to-end search illustrates how automated screening focuses computationally intensive substructure analyses on a few promising systems. Coupling multimodal agents to explicit forward modeling thus enables accurate, survey-scale lens analysis from macro mass profiles to small-scale dark matter structure.

arxiv.org/abs/2611.33404.title: Planetary biotechnospheres, biotechnosignatures and the search for extraterrestrial intelligence
arxiv.org/abs/2611.33404.excerpt:
arXiv:2611.33404v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The concept of planetary intelligence as collective intelligence is used to consider possible evolutionary paths of biotechnospheres that emerge on the intersection of the technosphere with the biosphere and support coupling of the technosphere with the biosphere, thus affecting planetary evolution. In mature biotechnospheres, the intelligence of technologies and the intelligence of life forms, including engineered life forms, could act in concert to perform various tasks (e.g. monitoring and restoring planetary environments and biodiversity; supporting space missions; terraforming cosmic objects). Space exploration can expand biotechnospheres beyond planets and create cosmic ecosystems. Humankind, other civilizations or their intelligent machines may produce biotechnosignatures (i.e. observables and artefacts of biotechnospheres) in the Solar System and beyond. I propose ten possible biotechnosignatures and strategies for the search for these biotechnosignatures in situ and over interstellar distances. For example, if a non-human advanced civilization existed and built biotechnospheres on Earth in the past, the descendants of its engineered bacteria could currently exist on Earth and have properties pertaining to the functions of the ancient bacteria in the biotechnospheres; intelligent technologies created by the ancient civilization could migrate to the Solar System's outer regions; these two scenarios are described as the Cosmic Descendants hypothesis. Interstellar asteroids, free-floating planets, spacecraft and objects gravitationally bound to flyby stars might carry extraterrestrial biotechnospheres and pass through the Solar System. In connection to the fate of post-main-sequence stars and their Oort clouds, the probability for interstellar asteroids to carry biotechnospheres or to be interstellar spacecraft is estimated as very low.

arxiv.org/abs/2611.33419.title: Photometric Uncertainty Correction for Time-Domain Surveys: Vera C. Rubin Data Preview 2 Case Study
arxiv.org/abs/2611.33419.excerpt:
arXiv:2611.33419v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Time-domain science, from variability detection to supernova cosmology, relies on accurate photometric uncertainties. We present a data-driven, catalog-level method to validate and improve the photometric uncertainties reported by time-domain surveys. The analysis is based on transforming light curves of non-variable objects into mean-variance whitened signals. We then estimate a correction to the uncertainties by matching the distribution of the whitened signals of all objects to the standard normal distribution, which they ought to follow when the uncertainties are correct. The correction can be modeled as a function of each measurement's flux, reported uncertainty, and available observational metadata, and can be applied to measurements of both non-variable and variable objects. Applied to the Rubin Observatory Data Preview 2 (DP2), the method shows that the uncertainties of bright sources are underestimated by up to a factor of five. The inferred corrections correspond to a magnitude error floor of about 10 mmag for both direct-image and difference-image photometry, decreasing to about 6 mmag in deeper fields. We provide the corrected uncertainties as part of the Rubin DP2 HATS catalogs.

arxiv.org/abs/2611.33435.title: A Variability Metric Pipeline for AGN studies
arxiv.org/abs/2611.33435.excerpt:
arXiv:2611.33435v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Variability in active galactic nuclei (AGNs) is remarkably diverse, spanning multiple timescales, wavelengths, and physical processes. Variability probes accretion physics and the interplay between supermassive black holes and their surroundings. Building on early case studies, the field has shifted toward population-level analyses of increasingly large datasets, making scalable techniques crucial for upcoming time-domain surveys. We developed a Python-based pipeline to analyze AGN light curves using variability metrics and applied it to 14,061 nearby AGNs ($z\lesssim 0.09$) observed with ZTF. We examined metric distributions and correlations. Amplitude-based metrics (e.g., $F_{\rm var}$) help identify major flares but are sensitive to single deviant epochs. Temporal metrics such as $\eta$ provide a complementary check. Comparison with WISE infrared photometry suggests that $\eta$ traces the strength of AGN activity.
